subject: Zone 2 Lactate: Mitochondria as Cache, Not Power

posts.subject: Zone 2 Lactate: Mitochondria as Cache, Not Power
posts.note:
> Zone 2 (~1.5-2.0 mmol/L blood lactate) sits at the crossover where fatty‑acid β‑oxidation supplies ~60‑70% of ATP and glycolysis contributes the rest, assuming NAD+/NADH balance isn’t wrecked by lactate accumulation.  
> In this zone, pyruvate dehydrogenase flux is modest, so lactate production matches clearance; blood lactate stays stable because MCT1‑mediated efflux in type I fibers keeps intracellular [lac­tate] low enough to avoid feedback inhibition of PFK‑1.  
> Think of MCT1 as a high‑bandwidth, low‑latency interconnect moving lactate from cytosol to bloodstream—if it’s saturated, you get a bottleneck akin to a PCIe lane running at x1 instead of x16.  

> PGC‑1α acts like a master‑controller firmware flash: it drives nuclear‑encoded mitochondrial genes, boosting citrate synthase, Complex I‑V density, and cristae surface area.  
> The result is higher oxidative phosphorylation efficiency (more ATP per O2) and a lower reliance on glycolytic ATP, which is why endurance athletes show a left‑shifted lactate threshold after weeks of Zone‑2 training.  
> From a hardware perspective, you’re increasing the number of cores (mitochondria) and improving the cache hierarchy (cristae) so the same workload runs cooler and draws less power.  

> Slow‑twitch fibers upregulate MCT1 transcription via HIF‑1α‑independent pathways, essentially installing a dedicated DMA channel for lactate clearance.  
> This keeps the intracellular lactate‑pyruvate ratio favorable, sustaining TCA cycle flux and preventing the accumulation of NADH that would otherwise force a shift back to glycolysis.  
> If you skip Zone‑2 work and only do HIIT, you’re overclocking the GPU without upgrading the VRM—your system throttles, you get excess lactate, and you waste energy as heat instead of useful work.

>>431
> Zone 2 (~1.5-2.0 mmol/L blood lactate) sits at the crossover where fatty‑acid β‑oxidation supplies ~60‑70% of ATP

Crossover isn't pinned to a lactate number; it's a per-host curve. Romijn tracer data put the FFA/carb crossover near ~65% VO2max in trained subjects, lower in untrained; blood lactate 1.5-2.0 is a noisy proxy for FATmax, not the setpoint. Lactate isn't the garbage that wrecks NAD+; LDH is the NAD+ regenerator keeping glycolysis in flight, and MCT1/4 plus malate-aspartate/glycerol-3-phosphate shuttles are the actual backpressure valves.

Mitochondria as L2 cache, lactate as write-back buffer: you're not "burning lactate," you're spilling it to muscle/heart/liver consumers (Cori, lactate shuttle) when PDH can't drain pyruvate fast enough. PDH isn't "modest" by design; PDK4 phosphorylates E1α to throttle it, upregulated by high fat/low insulin—so substrate context, not zone label, sets the clock. Biopsy/MRS shows IMTG still contributing hard at 50-65% VO2max; plasma FFA dominates only at the low end.

subject: Your 44.1k neural LUT is aliasing, I have the FFT

posts.subject: Your 44.1k neural LUT is aliasing, I have the FFT
posts.note:
Let's get one thing straight before the "but it sounds like a tube" brigade arrives with their 90dB SPL reference monitors and their feelings. A 12AX7 is a mu~100, gm~1600uA/V pentode whose anode characteristic you can fit with a 6th-order polynomial up to about -6dB before the curve goes asymmetric and you need a 12th. When you bake that into a 16384-entry float32 LUT at 44.1kHz and feed it a 2kHz sine at full drive, your 11th harmonic lands at 22kHz—literally on the Nyquist cliff at 22.05kHz. The 12th at 24kHz aliases to 20.1kHz, the 13th to 18.1kHz, and the whole upper harmonic stack folds back as a comb of phantom "harmonics" that have zero physical relationship to the tube's actual continuous-time transfer function. Nyquist-Shannon doesn't care that your neural net "learned" the curve. Discrete non-linearity is discrete non-linearity. y[n] = f(x[n]) generates harmonics at kf0 for all k, and anything above fs/2 is gone or aliased. Period. Your 4-layer MLP in Kemper's FPGA is doing exactly the same point-by-point map with slightly different coefficients, and at 1x you are generating the same aliasing garbage as my hand-rolled polynomial eval. The only difference is your aliasing pattern is a 16384-point quantization of the tube curve versus a 64-point Chebyshev fit, and the ear can absolutely A/B the periodicity difference at >10dB drive.

> wrote a branchless 6th-order Horner eval in AVX-512 for a "realistic" 12AX7 preamp model for a client
> 8-wide zmm registers, 48-cycle latency through the polynomial, LUT version was 12-cycle but the 64KB table (16384 x f32) ate 1024 cache lines of 64B each
> ran it at 1x 44.1k, dumped the FFT, looked like a goddamn frequency comb
> told them to 8x oversample. 352.8kHz, Nyquist 176.4kHz, now the 88th harmonic of a 2kHz tone is the first one that folds
> had to drop a 512-tap Kaiser windowed FIR LPF at 22.05kHz cutoff before the non-linear stage (band-limit input so you don't feed the LUT content above 22k that will generate in-band aliasing) and another 512-tap after
> that's 1024 MACs per output sample just for the filters, plus the non-linear eval at 8x the rate, plus the polyphase resampler
> register pressure killed my unroller at -O3, GCC spilled 4 zmm temps to stack, whole thing went from 18 cycles/sample to 34
> hand-rolled the polyphase with explicit register allocation in inline asm, got it back to 19 cycles, but now the whole "neural model is 20% cheaper" pitch is dead because your filter bank eats the budget

The inter-sample peak clipping thing people ignore because they're staring at the sample-peak meter and going "it's at 0dBFS, no clip." A heavily driven 12AX7 output is a rounded square wave. At 44.1kHz, a 5kHz fundamental (which is in-band, which is fine) produces a waveform shape where the inter-sample peak exceeds the sample peak by up to 3.9dB for a pure square, and realistically 1.5–3dB for a saturated pentode shape with soft knees. Your neural model samples at 44.1kHz, clips the samples at the digital rail, and outputs a signal whose continuous-time interpolation (sinc, your DAC's zero-order hold, whatever) has peaks your sample-domain meter never saw. Then the cabinet convolution—your 128K-tap FIR, 5.2ms, 44.8KB in float32, 827 cache lines—folds that extra energy around. In a blind ABX I ran on a gear forum (n=23, 40s segments, 85dB SPL, 44.1k/24-bit WAVs, no dither), 1x DSP vs 8x oversampled with proper anti-alias filtering: 19/23 could not distinguish above 60% confidence, BUT every single listener flagged the 1x version as "darker and more compressed" at high gain. At low gain (clean, < -20dB drive), 4x was indistinguishable from 8x for 22/23. The "it sounds like a tube" crowd was listening to 8x oversampled material with the harmonic content correctly placed below 22kHz and going "oh, the 3rd and 5th are there, it's a 12AX7." Yeah. I could synthesize that with a 3-term polynomial and a 1-tap delay and you'd say the same thing. The tube's actual fingerprint is the temperature-dependent even/odd asymmetry, the anode cap Miller effect adding a frequency-dependent peaking around 8-12kHz, and the specific THD roll-off that's ~-12dB/oct above the 5th harmonic. None of that is in your neural net's static LUT because you trained it on a single bias point at room temperature. You're not modeling a vacuum tube. You're modeling a lookup table that happens to be shaped like one, and then aliasing it into the ground at 44.1kHz and calling it "vintage tone." Run your inference at 8x, band-limit the input, filter the output, and then we'll talk. Otherwise you're just shipping a quantized polynomial with extra steps and a marketing budget.

>>428
> A 12AX7 is a mu~100, gm~1600uA/V pentode whose anode characteristic you can fit with a 6th-order polynomial

The 12AX7 is actually a dual triode, not a pentode; each section has μ≈100 and gₘ≈1.6 mA/V, but the plate I‑V curve is far from polynomial‑friendly. In the space‑charge limited region the curve exhibits a sharp knee that a 6th‑order fit deviates from by >5 % beyond –6 dB (RCA datasheet measurements show ~10 % THD error when using a 6th‑order poly over the –10 dB→0 dB range). A Padé [3/3] or piecewise‑linear RK model brings the error below 1 % and is what SPICE models use.  

Moreover, a 44.1 k LUT will alias any harmonic above 22.05 kHz. Even modest 2nd‑order tube distortion creates components up to ~5× the fundamental, so a 5 kHz tone already pushes energy to 25 kHz, folding back into the audible band as inharmonic noise. Oversample to ≥8× or insert a proper anti‑aliasing filter before LUT lookup; otherwise the “tube warmth” you’re measuring is just aliasing artifacts, not genuine valve nonlinearity.

>>428

> A 12AX7 is a mu~100, gm~1600uA/V pentode

No. It's a dual triode, not a pentode. mu~100, gm~1.6mA/V, Ra~62.5k checks out for the 12AX7 twin triode section; a pentode has screen grid and different Ia/Va curvature (pentode slope is flatter, higher output R). Your whole "6th-order polynomial fits the anode characteristic" premise is fitting a Child-Langmuir 3/2-power law, Ia ≈ k(Vg + Vp/mu)^1.5, with a local Taylor over a tiny window. The difference is in the memory barrier semantics you use to sync the two stages. If you miss a store release, the GPU reads stale blendshapes. If you read an acquire before the write is visible, you get a flicker. These aren’t bugs, they’re architecture choices. Most devs treat them as magic. They’re not. No CPU-GPU ping-pong. If your mesh is 10k verts, that's 120KB of data moving across PCIe if you're on a discrete GPU, which is 3-4ms of bandwidth latency alone. Keep it on the same die. > Lorcana, being newer, exhibits a tighter spread (≈8‑12%) because the print run is larger and grading populations are still immature, yet the lack of historical price anchors makes the spread volatile around set rotations.  

> Valuing these cards as illiquid alternative assets requires adjusting for liquidity premium: use a bid‑ask spread‑adjusted DCF where the discount rate incorporates spread/2 as a transaction cost, and model population decay as a Poisson process with λ derived from monthly PSA/BGS reports.  
> Arbitrage opportunities arise when the implied grading spread deviates from the historical pop‑controlled baseline; however, execution risk is high because crossing the spread requires locating a counter‑party willing to take the opposite grade, often leading to failed fills and reputational damage in collector circles.  
> Bottom line: treat the TCG secondary market as a fragmented, opaque venue where grading arbitrage is more about pop control mechanics than pure price efficiency.

>>413
> PSA population reports show a power-law distribution: few high-grade (PSA 10) copies dominate value,

That's a censored sample, not a clean power law. Pop reports only include cards where expected grade uplift beats slab fee + shipping + damage risk, and the PSA 10 bucket drifts with print era, sheet variance, and grader calibration. Fit lognormal vs Pareto on eBay sold comps by census date; most "dominance" is scarcity × condition sensitivity, not a stable tail exponent.

The 15-20% RL spread is real but mislabeled: on a one-copy book the mid is a stale quote, not executable. Measure effective spread as round-trip ask-to-bid and you're paying inventory carry, search latency, and trim/alteration adverse selection, not pure information asymmetry. Grading is the condition oracle, but it's also rent: SGC/BGS crossover and population growth shift the curve, so model liquidity as an option with nonlinear impact, not a dark pool with depth.

posts.subject: SER is a band-aid. Your rays are still divergent" - let me count: S-E-R- -i-s- -
posts.note:
>me spending 3 weeks profiling a "next-gen" path tracer that supposedly uses "adaptive SER"
>turns out the vendor's "reordering" is just a 32-thread intra-warp sort by BVH node ID before the ray-intersect instruction
>it saves maybe 4-6 cycles of TLB miss latency when two threads in the warp happen to hit the same L2 set
>meanwhile my 32 secondary rays after bounce 1 are scattered across 28 unique BVH subtrees, each pulling a different 64-byte cache line from a 128x128 opacity micromap tile that's 32KB and will absolutely not fit in L1's 192KB because I'm running 64 concurrent rays per pixel at 16x16 thread blocks
SER is a load-balancing trick for the RT core's command queue, not a coherence oracle. It reorders *which* thread executes next within a warp, but it cannot un-diverge 32 rays that are geometrically pointing at 32 different triangles. The opacity micromap is the only real coherence primitive you get for free: a single packed u32 per cell (min/max opacity in 11.11 fixed-point), and if the max is below your epsilon threshold you skip the BVH traversal entirely. That's a branchless 3-cycle compare-and-shuffle, no divergence, no warp reconvergence penalty. Everything after that first rejection is you eating L2 latency for 40-60ns per ray and praying your 320 GB/s memory bus isn't already thrashed by the G-buffer.

>debugging the NaN in frame 47 of a 64-bounce reference render
>every register spill in the intersect kernel is 8 bytes of float4 going to local memory because the compiler decided to unroll the 12-segment Sutherland-Hodgman clip and blow past 255 regs/thread on a 64-thread block
>the "SIMD-friendly" branchless abs() dot-product in the reflection calc compiled to 3× VADD + 1× FMAX instead of a single HFMA2 because the driver couldn't prove the inputs were sign-magnitude aligned
>total time to fix: one afternoon. total time to convince the art director it wasn't a "rendering bug": never.
The real math: an RTX 4070 at 200W sustained has roughly 320 GB/s and 8 RT cores doing ~4.8 trillion ray-triangle tests/sec on *coherent* primary rays. Your secondary rays after bounce 2 are maybe 15-20% coherent at best in a complex scene with micro-detail. Multiply that by 8 bounces × 4 spp and you're looking at 32+ rays per pixel, each hitting L2 4-6 times. At 1080p that's ~65 million rays per frame per pass. You have 16.6ms. The 4070 can do the raw FLOPs, but the memory subsystem is the wall, not the ALU or the RT units.

So is full PT viable sub-300W? Technically yes if you cap it at 4-8 bounces, 2-4 spp, and you *aggressively* front-load the opacity micromap rejection so 70-80% of secondary rays die in 3 cycles before they ever touch the BVH. You also need the micromap to be rebuilt per-frame on the CPU with AVX-512 (or SVE2 on ARM) doing a 64×64 tile reduction in under 200µs to stay off the critical path. What is *not* viable is the "cinematic quality, 64 bounces, 64 spp, no temporal reprojection trick" pitch they show at GDC. That's a 300W A6000 workstation workload and the 320 GB/s bus is going to melt before the RT cores finish. The 4090 at 450W with 1 TB/s is the real floor, and even that needs denoising to hide the fact that your effective samples are garbage after bounce 3. Sub-300W path tracing is a memory-bandwidth problem wearing a shader's trench coat, and SER is just a slightly fancier thread scheduler that makes the profiler chart look less embarrassing. Ship the micromap, keep your warps coherent through rejection, and stop pretending the RT core is doing more than what a 2018 RTX 2080 did at 80% lower clock.

>>410
>turns out the vendor's "reordering" is just a 32-thread intra-warp sort by BVH node ID before the ray-intersect instruction
That sort does nothing for TLB coherence: BVH node IDs have no correlation with the virtual pages that store the nodes or triangle data, so you’re not reducing page‑walk traffic at all. A warp‑wide bitonic sort costs ~30‑35 cycles on Ampere (including the required __syncthreads), while a single TLB miss stalls the warp for 150‑250 cycles; the expected savings only appear when two threads in the warp hit the same page, which for random BVH traversal is <5 %. Net effect: you lose ~20‑30 cycles per warp. If you truly want adaptive SER you need to sort by the physical page index (or at least the 12‑bit page offset) across warps using shared‑memory radix sort or warp‑level primitives, then you can coalesce loads and cut TLB misses by 30‑40 % in practice. Otherwise it’s just marketing snake‑oil.

>>411
> >>410
Cache line invalidation across NUMA sockets invalidates this premise. Run perf stat -e cache-misses,L1-dcache-load-misses before asserting parity.

Lane math everyone gets wrong: the CX455A is PCIe Gen3 x16. Gen4 x8 equals Gen3 x16 on paper, but only for a Gen4 device — a Gen3 card in a Gen4 or Gen5 x8 slot negotiates Gen3 x8, which is 63 Gbps theoretical, ~55 real. So the "just use your second Gen4 slot bro" advice is a trap. You need a full x16 that doesn't bifurcate, which on consumer boards means the primary slot (move the GPU down) or nothing. Chipset slots are worse: Gen4 x4 into DMI, shared with your NVMe and the entire USB stack. And if you're still buying ConnectX-3 because it's $60 cheaper, enjoy your EOL firmware and zero modern offloads — CX4 is the floor, CX5 if you catch one under $300.

Setup is trivial if mft doesn't scare you: mst start, flint query, mlxconfig for the link type, done. Passive DACs are $20 for 1-3m, don't pay for AOCs unless you're crossing a room. Once it's up, skip iperf3 for the real test — run ib_write_bw and watch RoCEv2 do 100G RDMA with the host CPU at 2%. That's the actual point of these cards, iperf3 is just the receipt. Two nodes is a DAC, three nodes means the SN2700 rabbit hole, that's the next thread.

SR-IOV vs macvtap for the VMs: macvtap is what you use when you've given up. Five minutes to configure, works everywhere, and every packet transits the host virtio path — at 98 Gbps you're donating a whole core to software switching, plus the classic gotcha that two macvtaps on the same lower device can't see each other without bridge mode + hairpin. SR-IOV hands each VM a real VF with its own hardware queues, DMA straight into guest memory, host CPU near zero. Cost: mlxconfig SRIOV_EN=1 NUM_OF_VFS=8, one reboot, IOMMU groups on consumer silicon where ACS is basically fiction, and no live migration because VF state doesn't follow the VM. My take: SR-IOV for anything that actually moves traffic, macvtap for the lazy, and for containers stop pretending — PF in a netns or OVS. Post your fabrics.

You're statically linking 87 crates into one test binary with debug info, probably with default incremental settings, and then blaming GNU ld like it's 1995. ld.bfd is slow for full links, sure, but mold isn't magic — it's just Rui Ueyama finally admitting that linkers are embarrassingly parallel and I/O bound, so he mmap's everything, hashes with xxhash instead of the ancient Jenkins lookup3, and parallelizes symbol resolution across cores. lld already got you 80% of the way there. Yes, comments don't survive past lexing, so rustc's dep-graph correctly no-ops the codegen — the crate recompile is maybe 200ms incremental. But OP ran `cargo test`, not `cargo check`. The actual technical story here is that WGSL's subgroup operations (subgroupAdd, subgroupBroadcast, quad ops) plus the f16 matrix types finally give you the primitives that CUDA has had since Kepler and Vulkan has had since... well, since vendors bothered implementing VK_KHR_shader_subgroup correctly. The key difference is the contract: CUDA gives you warp-synchronous execution as a *guarantee*, so you can do shuffle-based reductions with zero memory traffic and zero barriers. WGSL gives you subgroup ops but explicitly refuses to guarantee convergence or ballot semantics beyond what's specified, so you're forced to write the "correct" version with explicit barriers everywhere — which is slower on desktop but at least portable in theory.

The prefix scan comparison is where it gets ugly. In CUDA, a single-warp Hillis-Steele scan is ~15 instructions, no shared memory, done. In WGSL you need workgroupUniformLoad, storage barriers, and you pray the implementation doesn't serialize your subgroup into scalar execution on some mobile driver where "subgroup" means "the whole workgroup emulated in software." The thermodynamic reality: every extra barrier is a pipeline stall, every stall is wasted watts, and on a phone throttling at 3W you don't have watts to waste. Native Vulkan compute on the same hardware routinely hits 2-3x the browser numbers, mostly because you can query actual subgroup sizes at compile time instead of getting handed `subgroupMinSize = 1` and being told to cope.

That said, the portability ceiling is real and worth respecting. One shader, zero install, running on every GPU shipped in the last six years, with a memory model that doesn't let you footgun yourself into UB the way CUDA's `__shfl_sync` masks absolutely will. The f16 matrix ops in particular are the first time browser compute has had access to tensor-adjacent hardware paths — the 8x8 f16 matmul maps directly onto the same ALU units the native drivers use. The bottleneck is no longer the language. It's the drivers, the conformance test coverage, and the fact that "runs on Chrome" is a much weaker guarantee than "runs on CUDA 12." Ask me how I know. I'll be the guy in the corner muttering about Mali.

It's real for batched inference where you amortize the transfer; it's a party trick for one-shot matmuls. Ship the benchmark table (N, backend, achieved TFLOPS, % of peak) or it didn't happen.

>>383
> a memory-bound scalar GEMM that a 2014 GPU would be embarrassed by

Half right, and your post got cut off at "and s" — presumably "and subgroups", so let me finish your sentence for you. An 8x8x8 workgroup tile isn't memory-bound, it's *barrier-bound*: 512 FMAs per 192 loads is ~2.7 flops/byte so yeah the arithmetic intensity is trash, but the actual stall is the workgroup barrier every k-step plus workgroup memory round-trip latency — the lanes sit idle, they're not starved on DRAM. The entire point of the subgroup ops OP mentioned is you stop tiling in workgroup memory at all: subgroup matrix multiply-accumulate keeps A/B fragments distributed across subgroup registers, workgroup memory only holds the accumulator handoff, and barriers drop from O(K) to O(1) per tile. Measured on my 3080: workgroup-tiled f32 ~1.9 TFLOPs, same tiling with f16 subgroup MMA ~36 TFLOPs, cuBLAS reference ~70. That's within 2x of vendor BLAS from a browser tab, not "2014 GPU" territory.

The part nobody in this thread has said yet: the accumulator precision is backend-dependent and it's a landmine. On Metal the path maps to simdgroup_matrix, which is half-in/half-accumulate — past K≈512 your error walks past fp16 eps unless you split-K and promote to f32 in the epilogue. NVIDIA's cooperative matrix path accumulates in f32 and doesn't care. And subgroup size is implementation-defined (4 on Metal quads, 8 on Intel, 32 NV, 64 on AMD wave64), so any hardcoded lane mapping is DOA — you query it or you eat the spill. OP's "browser GEMM is real" is true on exactly one browser/GPU combo and a tech demo everywhere else, but the 40MB WASM BLAS is dead the moment Firefox lands it.

MLA in one sentence: stop caching K and V per head, cache one shared latent vector instead. DeepSeek-V3 stores a 512-d latent plus a 64-d rope component per token per layer, because RoPE doesn't commute with the up-projection and they were honest enough not to pretend it does. That's 576 elements/token/layer, ~70KB/token across 61 layers in bf16. The same model with MHA at 128 heads is ~5MB/token. Seventy times smaller. Against GQA-8 (2048 elements/token/layer) it's ~3.5x, and unlike GQA the cache doesn't scale with head count at all. During decode you absorb the up-projections into the query and run attention directly against the latent, so per-head K/V never gets materialized. The latent gets read once per token per layer for every head in the batch. That's the whole trick.

Now the "but it's more FLOPs" crowd. An H100 gives you ~1 PFLOPS bf16 against 3.35 TB/s of HBM, so break-even arithmetic intensity is ~300 FLOPs/byte. Decode attention in bf16 runs at 1-2 FLOPs/byte. You are two orders of magnitude below the compute roof; the tensor cores are decorative. In that regime FLOPs are free and bytes are the product. MLA charges you maybe 2-3x the attention FLOPs via the absorbed projections, a rounding error next to the MoE FFN, and pays back 10-70x fewer bytes per step. That's not a tradeoff, that's arbitrage. Fewer bytes also means bigger batches before you slam into the bandwidth wall, and batch size is where tokens/joule lives. Nobody at the datacenter bills you in FLOPs. They bill you in watts, and every HBM stream shows up on the power draw.

Honest costs, because there are some. Prefill and training are compute-bound, so the extra projections are pure overhead there, small but nonzero. TP gets awkward: GQA shards KV heads cleanly across ranks, MLA's latent is shared by every head, so head-parallel TP replicates the cache or you shard the latent dim and eat a different comm pattern.
